synthesis.body: A shell loop that spawns a process per file (`for f in ...; do mkdir -p ...; cp -P ...; done`) looks cheap and is not: cost is spawns x per-spawn latency, and per-spawn latency is a property of the machine, not the repo. Measure it before optimising anything else — `time (for i in $(seq 1 1000); do /bin/echo -n; done)`. Dev machines running endpoint security have measured ~26ms per spawn here vs ~1ms on CI Linux, which is why a harness can take 30 min locally and 112s in CI. Rewriting one such loop (2 spawns x 3,100 files x 6 seedings) as a single stdlib-Python pass cut tools/test-pre-pr.sh from ~28-37 min to ~4-8 min. Two behaviours the shell gave implicitly must be re-added by hand: `cp -P` overwrites an existing destination but shutil.copy2(follow_symlinks=False) raises FileExistsError (unlink first), and a read loop handles arbitrary path bytes but bytes.decode() aborts on non-UTF-8 (use os.fsdecode). Also check whether `set -e` is actually in effect at the call site before relying on it to catch the new command's exit.

title: Per-file subprocess loops in test harnesses scale with spawn cost, not file size
